definition: Self-denial is the giving up or restraining of one’s own interests for the sake of another person or a valued purpose. In the historical source, it is the element of sacrifice that distinguishes stronger forms of generosity from mere fellow-feeling.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Generosity; pinned source text

reasons: The packet does not define the term "self-denial" itself; it defines "Generosity" and says generosity involves self-denial.
The claim that self-denial is "the element of sacrifice that distinguishes stronger forms of generosity from mere fellow-feeling" is not supported by the packet and overstates the historical source.
The phrasing turns a historical comparison into a general dictionary definition of self-denial, which is not justified by the source text.

The definition adds “valued purpose” as a target of self-denial, but the packet only explicitly frames self-denial within actions toward “others” (bestowal of goods or favours upon others; sacrificing an interest of our own to an equal interest of a friend or a superior).

The definition says “giving up or restraining” one’s own interests; the packet supports “sacrifice” and self-denial in generosity, but does not support “restraining” as a distinct element of the term in the provided text.
